summary:
In myth, the Sun and Moon were the two eyes of Horus. Two Eyes of Horus is a browser-based tool for rapid evaluation of lunar landing sites. Each site is judged by two “eyes”: the Sun eye for power and the Moon eye for the direct line to Earth. Users choose from 16 curated sites, including Apollo, CLPS and south pole targets, or enter any custom lunar coordinates.
Sun and Earth positions come from the astronomy-engine ephemeris (about 1 arcminute accuracy), rotated into the Moon’s frame using the IAU 2009 pole and liberation. For each of 360 azimuths, the tool computes a terrain skyline from LOLA topography out to 200 km, including the Moon’s curvature, with no atmospheric refraction.
It reports solar elevation, relative power, sunny share, Earth-in-view share, longest night, longest no-signal gap, and countdowns to sunset and Earthset over a 30-day window. A first-person surface view, a 3D space map, a horizon panorama and a clickable timeline make these results easy to read. Side-by-side comparison lets planners test alternative sites or dates in seconds. Rigorous enough for engineers and clear enough for the public, it shows at a glance where both eyes stay open.
details:
We used the ancient Egyptian tale of the Two Eyes of Horus to frame the problem: the Sun eye represents power, the Moon eye represents the link home, and Akhet, the horizon, marks where each opens or closes. A first-person perspective of the lunar sky simplifies raw ephemeris numbers, making them easy to interpret at a glance.

Our website is a tool that helps mission planners select the most suitable landing site and date for a Moon landing. It addresses two key factors: the "Sun eye"—determining when the Sun is above the horizon to provide energy to solar panels—and the "Moon eye"—determining when the Earth is visible, allowing for direct communication with Earth without the need for an intermediary satellite. By identifying the longest duration during which both "eyes" are open—meaning the Earth is visible at the same time the Sun is above the horizon—the tool helps pinpoint the optimal time for a landing.

To further aid the user, we have included a 3D map; by picking a place on the Moon, the user may see the dark lunar sky, the horizon line (Akhet), and the locations of the Sun and Earth as they would appear at that time. Users can also move their viewpoint and manipulate the timeline to see how these elements change over time.

Once a site is selected, a data table appears, containing information about that specific location, including: Sun height, Sun compass direction, Skyline in Sun direction, Sun above skyline by, Earth height / skyline, Earth disc / Sun disc, Sunset in, Earth stays up for, Sunny share, Earth-in-view share, Longest night and Longest no-signal gap.

It also contains three maps, the first of which is a 3D space map (not to scale): the Moon with the Sun (gold) and Earth (blue) in their true directions. Gold diamond = this site, red = the other site. Gold and blue lines turn bright when the Sun or Earth can be seen from the site. The far dots are the real planets Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. Drag to rotate.

The second graph relates to a "horizon map": the dark shape represents the horizon line, while the dots illustrate the paths of both the Sun (in gold) and the Earth (in blue) over a period of approximately 30 days.

The third graph includes a timeline: the timeline allows for changes to evolve over time, rather than being limited to a single moment.

Another feature of our web platform is the ability to compare two different landing sites. When this option is selected, the system compares the two landing sites, and the parameters is the same that used in one site , helping the user determine which site is the most suitable for landing at that particular time.

If a user is undecided or unsure which landing site to choose, they can click on the "Planner" . This takes them to a page listing all the sites registered on the platform, where they can select multiple landing sites to compare. Alternatively, if a desired landing site is not already in the system, the user can input its coordinates.

Once the sites are selected, the platform identifies the most appropriate landing site for the current moment and explains why it is the best choice by calculating the following for each of the selected locations: Power index (Sun height counts) ,Earth link (Moon eye open), Both eyes open, Longest both-open stretch, Longest darkness, Longest comms blackout and Sunlight (Sun eye open)

It also includes a timeline diagram for each site, which shows when the sun and moon will be visible throughout the day at each landing site.

 
Another feature of our site is its ability to test every start date within a given range for each landing site , identifying the period during which both "eyes" remain open for the longest duration.

This used to determine the most suitable time and site for landing.

Furthermore, once a site has been selected, we can compare multiple timeframes for the same landing site—a process specifically focused on pinpointing the optimal time for landing.

 

For new users, we have added a tab called "Help," which provides a simple explanation of how to use the website.

Benefits

Users can simply compare landing sites and dates in minutes using a variety of ways, all in one spot, rather than relying on several expert tools. They can make fast comparisons by looking at the "eyes" that represent the interplay of solar energy (the Sun) and the Earth.

Creativity

 We used the ancient Egyptian tale of the Two Eyes of Horus to frame the problem: the Sun eye represents power, the Moon eye represents the link home, and Akhet, the horizon, marks where each opens or closes. A first-person perspective of the lunar sky simplifies raw ephemeris numbers, making them easy to interpret at a glance.

Intended Impact

Mission planning on the Moon isn’t just for mission planners; our goal is to help anyone who wants to learn more about it—and to show why even a small change in ding site or date can significantly impact energy and communication.

Factors We Considered

We ensured the website is accessible to everyone by incorporating features that simplify the experience for beginners. For instance, we added visual indicators—represented by icons—that show when the sun is above the horizon (enabling the panels to generate energy) and when the Earth is in view (allowing for direct communication with Earth without the need for an intermediary satellite).

Additionally, we included a "Help" tab to guide new users on how to navigate and use the website.

We also took into account that not all users will be mission planners; therefore, we provided an option to display a simplified, less data-intensive view tailored for beginners. Furthermore, we ensured that all of the data we used was sourced from legitimate NASA resources, and we presented it in a variety of ways to make it more accessible to users.

 

Coding Languages and Hosting

The coding  languages used in this website are HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Python. The website is hosted on GitHub pages. The Repository were the Project files are stored can be accessed easily via this link.
